title: Caleb at eighty-five (Joshua 14:6–15)
hook: the old scout says he's as strong as ever: "give me this mountain"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zelophehad's five daughters, who asked for a portion of their own and got it. Your line was a place can be a calling. Did you make room for someone? Today, one old man asks for his. Day seven hundred seven.

Eighty-five years old, and he's asking for ground held by giants. The people of Judah have come to Joshua at Gilgal, where the land is being shared out. One old man steps forward with a story. Forty years old was I, he says, when Moses sent me to spy out this land. I brought back word as it was in my heart. The others made the people's hearts melt. I didn't. Then he names his age today. And then he makes a request, and it isn't for a quiet valley.
screen: `GILGAL: THE LAND IS SHARED OUT.` → `FORTY WHEN MOSES SENT ME.` → `EIGHTY-FIVE TODAY.`

segments.voice: Caleb's speech is mostly memory. Back in the wilderness, at Kadesh-barnea, Moses sent scouts into this land. The book of Numbers tells it: the others came back talking about walled cities and giants, the sons of Anak, and the camp lost its nerve. Caleb said, let us go up at once. Now, at Gilgal, he tells it in his own words, and one phrase keeps coming back: he wholly followed the Lord. He says it about himself. He quotes Moses saying it. And the narrator says it again at the end. Then the surprise. He says he's as strong today as the day Moses sent him, strong for war, for going out and for coming in. And he asks: "Now therefore give me this mountain." Not a settled valley. The hill country of Hebron, where the Anakim live, in cities great and fortified. The very people whose size frightened the scouts all those years ago. Caleb doesn't promise a victory. He says, maybe the Lord will be with me, and I'll drive them out. Notice the shape of it. The fear that froze a whole camp is the exact place he asks to go. He has carried that mountain in his mind for forty-five years. Joshua blesses him and gives him Hebron. The chapter ends quietly: the land had rest from war. The text doesn't make Caleb young again. It lets him be eighty-five, with a long memory and a hard request. Some readers hear a promise finally collected, since Moses swore the land his feet walked on would be his. Others hear something simpler: an old man who still wants a mountain to climb.
screen: `KADESH-BARNEA: THE SCOUTS LOSE NERVE.` · `HE WHOLLY FOLLOWED THE LORD.` · `AS STRONG NOW AS THEN.` · then, large: `GIVE ME THIS MOUNTAIN.` · then: `HEBRON IS HIS. THE LAND HAS REST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: start something, whatever your age. Sit comfortably, and let one thing come to mind that you've put off because you told yourself it was too late, or too early: a language, an instrument, a conversation, a walk you've never taken, a piece of work. Don't plan the whole mountain. Just look at it for a moment. Then choose the very first step, small enough to take this week, and hold it for the rest of the sit. Say Caleb's words under your breath: give me this mountain. The bell holds the time.
Anakim, the giants whose cities frightened the scouts forty-five years earlier, and whose hill country Caleb, at eighty-five, now asks Joshua to give him.

Your line: give me this mountain. Today, take the first small step toward something you thought you'd missed. And look back at this week: holy ground, the walls, Achan, the oath, the sun standing still, a place for everyone, and Caleb's mountain. Day seven hundred seven.

howItsDone: Jews read Caleb's request as part of Joshua, the opening book of the Prophets, and remember Caleb, with Joshua, as the scouts who did not lose heart in Numbers 13–14.

original.note: Hebrew: this mountain, from Caleb's request in Joshua 14:12.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old man claiming his reward.
what it means: at eighty-five, Caleb asks for the hill country of the Anakim, the place that once frightened the scouts.
what a scholar hears: wholly followed comes three times in Joshua 14:8, 9 and 14: Caleb's words, Moses' oath, the narrator.

sources.quoted: Now therefore give me this mountain

notes: Verify JPS 1917 wording of Joshua 14:12 'Now therefore give me this mountain' (certain in the KJV).
Ages forty and eighty-five and 'forty and five years' are from Joshua 14:7 and 14:10.
'Wholly followed' three times: Joshua 14:8, 14:9, 14:14; please confirm the count in JPS 1917.
Caleb's 'perhaps the Lord will be with me' paraphrases 14:12 ('it may be that the LORD will be with me').
Week-end look-back (days 701–707) is in the carry.
Caleb's conquest of Hebron and Achsah's request (Joshua 15:13–19) are left out.
